papers.title: Frequency-resolved decoherence spectroscopy of a semiconductor charge qubit coupled to a high-impedance resonator
papers.abstract: Superconducting resonators coupled to semiconductor quantum dots provide a powerful platform to investigate light-matter interaction and decoherence mechanisms in solid-state quantum systems. Here we study a hybrid circuit quantum electrodynamics architecture consisting of a GaAs double-quantum-dot charge qubit capacitively coupled to a high-impedance, frequency-tunable SQUID-array resonator. By tuning the qubit transition frequency over the range $ω_\mathrm{q}/2π\sim 3$-$6$ GHz, we perform frequency-resolved decoherence spectroscopy of the charge qubit across a broad energy window. Time-resolved measurements enable us to disentangle relaxation and pure dephasing processes and to identify distinct decoherence regimes as a function of qubit frequency. We find that at lower frequencies ($\leq 4.5$ GHz) dephasing dominates the qubit linewidth, whereas at higher frequencies energy relaxation becomes the leading contribution. The measured frequency dependence of the relaxation rate exhibits a cubic scaling, consistent with charge-qubit decay dominated by coupling to a piezoelectric phonon bath and providing frequency-resolved access to the corresponding phonon-induced spectral density. Our results show that hybrid semiconductor--superconducting circuits can serve as sensitive spectroscopic tools to probe microscopic decoherence mechanisms relevant for a wide range of hybrid quantum devices.

summary.summary: A GaAs double-quantum-dot charge qubit coupled to a frequency-tunable SQUID-array resonator enables frequency-resolved decoherence spectroscopy from 3 to 6 GHz, revealing a crossover from dephasing-dominated to relaxation-dominated decoherence. The measured relaxation rate exhibits cubic scaling with qubit frequency, consistent with piezoelectric acoustic phonon coupling and demonstrating the utility of tunable hybrid circuits as quantitative probes of microscopic dissipation.
summary.motivation: Charge qubits are sensitive probes of electrostatic noise but also suffer from phonon-induced relaxation; identifying which decoherence mechanism dominates at different qubit frequencies requires frequency-resolved measurements over a broad range while maintaining sufficient signal-to-noise ratio for time-domain analysis.
summary.method: We performed time-resolved measurements (Ramsey, Hahn-echo, relaxation) on a DQD charge qubit at the sweet spot $\varepsilon = 0$ across multiple tunnel-coupling configurations $2t/h = 3.7$–6.1 GHz, with the SQUID-array resonator tuned to resonance at each frequency to maintain high dispersive readout fidelity; master-equation fits to 2D spectroscopy data extracted $g_0/2\pi \approx 35$–60 MHz and $\Gamma_2$ values.
summary.result: At low frequencies ($\leq 4.5$ GHz), pure dephasing dominates with $\Gamma_\phi$ weakly frequency-dependent; at higher frequencies, relaxation becomes dominant and follows $\Gamma_1 \propto \omega_q^3$, consistent with piezoelectric phonon emission in GaAs. Peak cooperativity $C \approx 20$ is achieved at $\omega_q/2\pi = 3.71$ GHz with $g_0/\Gamma_2 \sim 10$.

papers.title: A K-band Kinetic Inductance Parametric Amplifier Near the Quantum Limit
papers.abstract: Advancing superconducting quantum devices to higher operating frequencies broadens their functionality and enables operation at elevated temperatures, but it also requires near-quantum-limited amplifiers beyond the few-gigahertz regime. Here we present a junction-free, kinetic-inductance parametric amplifier based on thin-film niobium nitride (NbN) operating at 23 GHz in the microwave K-band, achieving a gain up to 40 dB, a 100 MHz gain-bandwidth product, a 1 dB saturation input power of -85 dBm with 23 dB gain, and added noise no greater than 1.4 quanta for phase-preserving amplification. Leveraging the large superconducting gap of NbN, this architecture can be extended to even higher frequencies, supporting applications such as high-fidelity readout of millimeter-wave superconducting qubits and axion searches over an expanded mass window.

summary.summary: A junction-free kinetic-inductance parametric amplifier (KIPA) in NbN thin film operates at 23 GHz in the K-band, achieving 40 dB gain, 100 MHz gain-bandwidth product, and added noise $\leq 1.4$ quanta for phase-preserving amplification. The device demonstrates high saturation power of $-85$ dBm at 23 dB gain, enabling near-quantum-limited readout of millimeter-wave superconducting qubits and dark-matter searches at frequencies beyond conventional aluminum-based amplifiers.
summary.motivation: Advancing superconducting quantum devices to higher frequencies ($>10$ GHz) requires near-quantum-limited amplifiers, but aluminum (gap $\Delta \approx 40$ GHz) fundamentally limits conventional parametric amplifier designs; NbN with $T_c \approx 12.5$ K and larger superconducting gap enables operation in the K-band and beyond.
summary.method: A single-layer NbN resonator with parallel nanowires (50 nm $\times$ 1 μm $\times$ 25 nm, kinetic inductance $\sim 300$ pH per wire) coupled to a WR-42 waveguide supports four-wave mixing gain via two-tone or single-tone detuned pumping; noise is calibrated by monitoring signal-to-noise ratio degradation against a downstream HEMT amplifier (26 dB gain, $T_H \leq 10$ K).
summary.result: At $G_K = 23$ dB, saturation input power reaches $-85$ dBm (conservative lower bound); SNR measurements with interstage loss $\alpha \leq -7$ dB yield an upper bound on added noise of 1.4 photons, approximately 3 times the quantum limit, with nominal loss assumptions suggesting 0.7 quanta.

papers.title: A Dual Metastable-State Encoding Architecture for Quantum Processing with $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ Atom Arrays
papers.abstract: Neutral-atom arrays combine scalable qubit registers, long coherence times, flexible optical control, and strong Rydberg-mediated entangling interactions, making them a promising platform for quantum information processing. However, physical error rates remain a challenge, and fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires repeated mid-circuit measurement and reset of ancilla qubits without disturbing nearby data qubits. This requirement introduces significant control and architectural overhead, making qubit encoding an important architectural decision. Here, we propose a dual metastable-state qubit encoding for $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ atoms that utilizes two independent qubit subspaces in the $(6s6p)\,{}^3\mathrm{P}_0$ and $(6s6p)\,{}^3\mathrm{P}_2$ manifolds. The ${}^3\mathrm{P}_0$ manifold provides a long-coherence nuclear-spin (NS) qubit suitable for storage and arithmetic operations, while the ${}^3\mathrm{P}_2$ manifold provides a hyperfine-spin (HF) qubit, with $Δ_{\mathrm{HF}} = 2π\times 6.7~\mathrm{GHz}$, that enables fast Raman operations and direct state-selective imaging. Coherent shelving between the two metastable manifolds connects the qubit subspaces, allowing operations to be assigned to spectrally distinct processor zones. We simulate single-qubit and two-qubit gate fidelities in ${}^3\mathrm{P}_2$, as well as coherent shelving between the HF and NS qubit subspaces. We incorporate these physical-level estimates into an architectural resource estimation and logical-level simulation. Our approach integrates mid-circuit measurements and fast qubit operations within a single-species platform, providing a versatile framework for future fault-tolerant quantum computing with neutral-atom qubits.

similar_to.title: Demonstrating a long-coherence dual-rail erasure qubit using tunable transmons
Bias-preserving and error-detectable entangling operations in a superconducting dual-rail system

summary.summary: This paper proposes a dual metastable-state qubit encoding in $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ using the $(6s6p)\,{}^3\mathrm{P}_0$ and $(6s6p)\,{}^3\mathrm{P}_2$ manifolds to enable fast, mid-circuit quantum error correction in neutral-atom arrays. Through full master-equation simulations of gate operations and architectural resource estimation, the authors demonstrate that assigning the ${}^3\mathrm{P}_2$ manifold (with $\Delta_{\mathrm{HF}} = 2\pi \times 6.7$ GHz) to QEC and ${}^3\mathrm{P}_0$ to arithmetic logic reduces circuit overhead while maintaining fault-tolerant capabilities.
summary.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum error correction with neutral atoms requires repeated mid-circuit syndrome extraction on ancilla qubits without disturbing data qubits, imposing significant control overhead. A dual-manifold encoding within a single species can exploit distinct coherence and speed properties to separate these functions spectrally rather than spatially.
summary.method: The authors simulate single-qubit gates in ${}^3\mathrm{P}_2$ ($\mathcal{F}_{QB} = 99.916\%$ fidelity, $\Omega = 2\pi \times 2$ MHz), coherent shelving between manifolds via Raman transfer ($\mathcal{F}_{CS} = 99.936\%$), and $\mathcal{CZ}$ gates in Rydberg states, then compile benchmark circuits using a manifold-aware zone-aware compiler to estimate circuit duration and space-time volume for surface-code error correction.
summary.result: For code distances $d \in \{3,5,7\}$, assigning ${}^3\mathrm{P}_2$ to QEC and ${}^3\mathrm{P}_0$ to arithmetic reduces mid-circuit syndrome-extraction overhead and enables parallel execution across blocks; coherence times $T_1 = 1.44$ s and $T_2^* = 82.73$ ms in 850 nm tweezers support hundreds of QEC cycles, with projected logical error rates improving as the ${}^3\mathrm{P}_2$ two-qubit gate error decreases below $0.25\%$.
